  • Kernels do not capture values from the enclosing scope: KernelTransformer._check_names_bound (lang/lowering/checks.py) raises NameError instead.
  • Where Python's semantics are well defined and implementable, Tack adopts them deliberately: integer // and % floor like Python's, and floating ///% follow CPython's algorithm.

Costs and limits. Code that looks like Python can behave differently from Python, for example on integer overflow or on and of two numbers. The contract, not the Python reference manual, is the specification. Kernels need readable source, so a function created by exec() or typed into a bare REPL cannot be a kernel.

docs.title: 2. Translate or reject
docs.text:
Statement. Every construct the frontend sees is either translated according to its defined semantics or rejected with a diagnostic naming the construct, the function and the source position. Nothing is silently dropped.

Rationale. A dropped statement produces a kernel that compiles, runs and returns the wrong answer, which is the worst failure a numerical tool can have. An early version of the transformer did exactly this with assert (contract regression LC4).

Where it shows.

  • validate_source (lang/source_validation.py) checks the original kernel and device-function source with an allow-list visitor before lowering, including statements in unreachable code. It raises UnsupportedSyntaxError.
  • KernelTransformer.visit converts the transformer's own NotImplementedErrors into UnsupportedSyntaxError with a location, so any case the validator lets through and lowering cannot handle still fails loudly.
  • CallBindings (lang/call_bindings.py) resolves device calls statically and rejects calls that are neither a bound @tack.func nor an intrinsic.
  • Unsupported array dtypes are rejected by check_dispatch_types, never narrowed. Unsupported workgroup primitives and atomic types are rejected before compilation.
  • A statement with no defined execution count is rejected rather than run an arbitrary number of times: a store, atomic, barrier, block reduction or print outside the parallel loop raises UnsupportedSyntaxError at its source position (_check_outside_parallel_loop). Likewise a GPU launch longer than one grid can index raises ValueError (check_launch_size) instead of wrapping, and a kernel store to a read-only array is refused at dispatch.
  • verify_ir (lang/ir_verify.py) applies the same idea to the compiler itself: a pass that breaks an invariant stops the variant before code generation.

Costs and limits. The supported language is visibly smaller than Python, and some constructs users try first (keyword arguments, assert, comprehensions) are errors. Positions are in the dedented captured source, not absolute file coordinates. See Compilation Pipeline.

docs.title: 3. One kernel source; capabilities declared, not probed
docs.text:
Statement. A kernel's source is the same on all five backends. What differs between backends is described by declared capability attributes, which callers read instead of probing for methods or class names.

Rationale. Probing answers "is this method defined?", which is not the same question as "is this supported?". getattr(backend, 'supports_f64', True) once reported True for Metal, which has no f64 at all, because the attribute existed only on Level Zero. A missing memory_space() method made tack.memory_space() answer "cpu" for a Level Zero device pointer. A declaration states what is supported.

Where it shows.

  • Backend (packages/tack-core/src/tack/runtime/backend.py) declares name, ordinal, display_name/label, supported_dtypes, supports_device_reductions, supports_workgroups, device_options, device_memory_spaces and dlpack_refusal_note, and derives memory_domain.
  • Anything derivable is derived, so it cannot disagree with its source: supports_f64 is f64 in supported_dtypes, and supported_atomic_dtypes intersects a per-target table with supported_dtypes. Level Zero sets supported_dtypes in __init__ because f64 support depends on the device.
  • A single shared IR and pass pipeline (resolve_variant in runtime/kernel_utils.py) feeds five code generators. Device-dependent lowering choices, such as software texture sampling on HIP and Level Zero devices without image support, are made before the variant key is built, so they stay visible to the cache.

Costs and limits. Portability is bounded by the least capable backend for any given feature: Metal has no f64, the CPU has no workgroups, and atomic types vary by target. A kernel that uses such a feature is rejected on backends without it rather than emulated. A few places still identify backends by class name, notably inspect_kernel._generate_source when choosing a generator. See Backend Capabilities.

docs.title: 4. Specialize, and key everything you specialize on
docs.text:
Statement. Tack compiles a separate variant for each combination of facts it bakes into generated code, rather than generating generic code that reads those facts at run time. Every such fact is part of the variant key.

Rationale. Baking in dtypes, vector widths, template constants and row strides lets LLVM and the vendor compilers fold and vectorize around known values, and keeps generated code simple. But specialization is only correct if the cache key names everything that was baked in. The alternative, a key that misses something, has produced silent wrong numbers three times: a cache keyed on id(kernel), a key without the row stride, and a key without vector widths (LC3).

Where it shows.

  • kernel_variant_key and shape_signature (runtime/kernel_utils.py) build the key from argument types and categories, vector widths, template structure, baked-in dimensions and the CPU disjoint bit.
  • ir_shape_deps excludes the outermost loop's bound, which is passed at launch, so the most common kernel shape compiles once for every length.
  • _ClassToken (lang/kernel.py) keys template classes by identity without keeping them alive.
  • IR templates are immutable and passes run on a clone_ir copy, so one variant's resolution cannot leak into another.

Costs and limits. Variants multiply, and each pays a cold compile. A dimension used inside the kernel body specializes on every value, so open-ended shape sets need the length passed as a scalar. Template array shapes are keyed in full, which is stricter than necessary. See Specialization and Caching.

docs.title: 5. Correct by default; speed by measured opt-in
docs.text:
Statement. The default compilation preserves the defined behavior of every race-free program. Faster code that depends on an extra assumption is used only where that assumption has been checked for the call at hand, and only where it has been measured to help.

Rationale. A numerical framework that is fast but occasionally wrong cannot be trusted for anything. The original Tack made three unsafe promises: array pointers were marked noalias/restrict unconditionally, CUDA and Metal compiled with fast math, and custom LICM and CSE moved loads without memory or control-flow analysis. Each was removed when a case was found where it changed results (regressions LC1 and LC2; the Metal fast-math folds are listed in the contract's floating-point policy).

Where it shows.

  • Aliasing. Arrays may overlap, and no generated parameter carries an unconditional no-alias promise (LLVMCodeGen in codegen/llvm_gen.py, the C-family generators, and Metal's argument buffer).
  • Measured opt-in. The CPU backend compiles a second, noalias variant used only for calls whose written arrays arrays_disjoint proves do not overlap any other array. The check runs on every dispatch, and the result is part of the variant key.
  • Floating point. CUDA compiles with --ftz=false --prec-div=true --prec-sqrt=true --fmad=true and without --use_fast_math; Metal sets fastMathEnabled to false; HIP limits contraction to one expression (-ffp-contract=on), since hipRTC's default fused across statements and gave one variable two values; the CPU emits no LLVM fast-math flags. See the floating-point policy.
  • Optimization. optimize_ir (lang/ir_optimize.py) performs only conservative copy propagation; LICM and CSE stay disabled until they have the analyses they need.

Costs and limits. Safe defaults cost throughput in some kernels: an accumulation through an array that may alias cannot be kept in a register, and the contract notes that leaving fast math off may change throughput as well as low-order bits. The disjoint-array check adds a small cost to every CPU dispatch, and whether it pays depends on the host. Users cannot currently opt into fast math or declare no-alias themselves. See Memory and Aliasing and Numerical Semantics.

docs.title: 6. Measure runtime policy instead of hard-coding it
docs.text:
Statement. Decisions that depend on the machine and the kernel are made from measurements taken at run time, not from constants chosen on one developer's machine.

Rationale. The CPU backend's decision to spread a loop over threads is the clearest case. The crossover between serial and threaded execution moves by orders of magnitude with a kernel's arithmetic intensity, so no single element count is right. A fixed threshold made mid-size dispatches of cheap kernels slower than running them serially.

Where it shows.

  • Each compiled CPU kernel keeps a smoothed estimate of its serial cost per element (ns_per_elem), from which the backend derives parallel_min_elems, so the hot path is one integer comparison.
  • The backend measures its own fan-out cost (_fan_out_ns, in CPUBackend._calibrate_fan_out) by dispatching empty ranges through the real path, which runs no iterations and so has no side effects.
  • TACK_CPU_THREADS remains as an explicit override.

Costs and limits. Measured policies are harder to reason about and to test than constants, and they need care to keep measurement off the critical path and robust to noise. Their behavior can vary from run to run on a loaded machine. See CPU Threading Policy.

docs.title: 7. Correctness is defined by oracles
docs.text:
Statement. A result is correct when it matches an independent oracle, not when it matches what Tack produced before. Tests compare against arithmetic computed outside the compiler.

Rationale. Recording current output as the expected value freezes bugs in place. Several of the defects behind the contract's regression baseline were found only by comparing against an independent computation.

Where it shows.

  • packages/tack-core/tests/test_compiler_contract.py holds the LC1–LC8 regression baseline. Its expected values come from simple arithmetic or NumPy, not from recorded Tack output.
  • test_differential.py runs the same source as a compiled kernel and as serial Python over NumPy arrays, including generated programs with branches, break, continue and varying bounds. It exposed eager guarded calls, delayed operand loads and repeated augmented-store indices.
  • test_integer_expression_differential.py checks generated fixed-width integer expressions against an oracle written from the contract's rules, using nothing from the production compiler.
  • test_float_semantics.py uses exact rational arithmetic (Fraction) to accept either the separately rounded or the fused result where contraction is permitted, and nothing else.
  • Hardware validation is recorded per backend with device, runtime versions and pass/fail counts; a skip or deselection is not counted as validation.

Costs and limits. Oracles cover what they model. The differential tests exclude atomics, cooperative workgroups, vector methods and open numerical cases, and CPU validation does not establish GPU correctness. See Conformance and Validation.

docs.title: Where the principles pull against each other
docs.text:
• Specialization versus cold-start cost. Baking facts in makes warm code faster but multiplies compiles. Verification at every pass boundary (principle 2 applied to the compiler) adds to each one. Tack accepts a slower first call in exchange for a fast and correct warm path, and the disk cache pays it once per machine rather than once per process: its keys name what was baked in, as the variant key does, plus every name lowering resolved, so an edited device function or constant compiles again (see Specialization and Caching).
  • Correctness versus speed. The disjoint-array variant shows the intended resolution: keep the safe default, and add a faster path only where a per-call check proves the extra assumption, with the result in the cache key.
  • Portability versus capability. Declared capabilities let a kernel fail clearly on a backend that cannot run it, but they do not make it run there. Tack rejects rather than emulates, apart from a few lowering fallbacks (software texture sampling) that preserve the same semantics.

docs.title: Specialization and Caching
docs.text:
A Tack kernel is not compiled once. It is compiled once per variant: a specialization for one combination of the facts that the compiler bakes into generated code. This page defines what a variant is, lists exactly what goes into its key and why, describes the cache that holds variants and how long they live, and gives the user-facing consequences.

The governing requirement is in the contract's Specialization and compilation identity section: reusing compiled code must have the same defined behavior as compiling the current call independently. Every fact baked into code or its calling convention must therefore be part of the key. Conversely, runtime scalar values and the outer launch length alone should not force a recompile.

docs.title: What a variant is
docs.text:
KernelVariant in packages/tack-core/src/tack/runtime/kernel_utils.py holds one compiled specialization:

Attribute Contents ir the post-pass IR (before GPU scalar packing), kept so the launch range can be evaluated on every dispatch without rerunning passes payload whatever the backend's build callback returned: the JIT'd function on the CPU; the compiled kernel, pack_info and pack buffers on GPU requires_full_workgroups whether every launch must be a multiple of 256 lanes atomic_targets atomic parameter indices and their alignments, rechecked against each call's storage written_arrays (index, name) of each array argument the kernel may store to, so a dispatch can refuse read-only storage without walking IR has_textures whether any argument is a Texture3D, so a call without one skips rebinding textures dispatch_lock serializes dispatches of this variant on CUDA and HIP, whose payload holds the scalar pack buffers

Variants are produced and looked up only by resolve_variant(), the single entry point all five backends share. The Compilation Pipeline page describes the steps that build one.

docs.title: Two caches, two keys
docs.text:
Specialization happens at two levels, because some facts change what the frontend emits and others only change what the passes resolve. Both levels are also kept on disk, across processes (below), and in front of them a repeated call skips key derivation altogether (the dispatch fast path).

flowchart LR
    K["Kernel object"] --> IRC["IR template cache<br/>Kernel._ir / Kernel._ir_cache<br/>key: vector widths, texture extents,<br/>template structure"]
    K --> VC["Variant cache, one per backend<br/>backend._cache[kernel][variant_key]<br/>key: param types and categories, vector widths,<br/>template key, shape signature, disjoint bit"]
    IRC -- "template (immutable)" --> VC
Cache Owner Key Built by IR template Kernel (lang/kernel.py) Kernel._make_cache_key(vector_arrays, template_args, texture_arrays, debug), or none at all for the plain Kernel._ir (no vectors, textures or templates, debug mode off) template rewrite, source validation, AST transform, verify_ir('lowered') Compiled variant each backend instance (backend._cache) kernel_variant_key(...) clone, IR passes, verification, codegen, native compile

Every input to the IR template key also reaches the variant key, either directly (vector widths, template structure) or indirectly (texture extents arrive as _texture_shape on the parameter and, through each IRTextureSample, in the shape signature; debug mode's template has two more parameters, the hidden errors and extents arrays, so its parameter signature differs). Two calls that share a variant therefore always share an IR template.

Debug mode. tack.set_debug(True) (or TACK_DEBUG=1) lowers every kernel with bounds checks (lang/ir_bounds.py): ("debug",) leads the IR template key, and the two hidden array parameters follow the kernel's own. The extents are read from an array at run time rather than resolved, so a debug kernel compiles no variant per array length. With debug mode off, the IR and generated code are those of a build without the feature.

docs.title: The variant key, element by element
docs.text:
kernel_variant_key(ir_func, kernel, vector_arrays, template_args, shape_sig, disjoint) returns a five-tuple:

(param_sig, vec_sig, tmpl_key, shape_sig, disjoint)

The kernel itself is not in the tuple: each kernel has its own slot in the cache (see below).

docs.title: param_sig: types and categories
docs.text:
One entry per IR parameter, computed in a single pass because it runs on every dispatch:

(p.type_annotation, p._is_array, p._is_texture, p._texture_shape)

These come from infer_param_types (lang/type_inference.py) and the backend's store_texture_shapes, run on a private _KeyProbe rather than on the shared template (see Concurrency).

Component Values What it bakes in type_annotation an array's dtype; for a Python int/np.integer, i32, i64 or u64 chosen by integer_type_for_value from the value; for a float/np.floating, f32, or f64 when any array argument is f64 every expression's type, the arithmetic emitted, the C/LLVM parameter type, the pack buffer an argument lands in _is_array array (or texture) versus scalar the calling convention: pointer versus value on the CPU; buffer binding versus packed scalar on GPU _is_texture hardware texture versus not sampler code versus loads; HIP and Level Zero set it to False to choose software sampling when the device has no image support or the extent exceeds its 3-D image limit _texture_shape Texture3D.shape_3d the extents used in sampling code

docs.title: vec_sig: vector widths
docs.text: tuple(sorted(vector_arrays.items())): the component count of each tack.Array with a vector element dtype argument. Width determines how many component loads the frontend emits and the stride between vectors, so two widths need two lowerings and two compiled kernels. Leaving width out of the key once let a width-2 variant serve a width-3 call and return wrong norms; that is contract regression LC3.

docs.title: tmpl_key: template structure and constants
docs.text:
For calls with @tack.device_class arguments, Kernel._make_cache_key contributes one part per template parameter:

("tmpl_<index>",
 _ClassToken,                                   # identity of the class
 ((name, type(v), bits_or_value), ...),         # class-level constants
 ((name, dtype, shape, vector_n), ...),         # array attributes
 (runtime_attr_name, ...))                      # instance scalar names

(plus a leading ("vec", …) part when vector arrays are present).

  • Class identity. Two classes with the same name can have different methods, so the actual class is keyed, through a _ClassToken (below) rather than the class object itself.
  • Constants. Class-level numeric attributes are inlined as literals, so their values belong in the key. Each is stored with its Python type (1 and 1.0 lower differently). Floats are stored as their struct.pack('!d', v) bit pattern, which distinguishes 0.0 from -0.0 and gives NaN a key equal to itself despite NaN != NaN. An instance attribute that shadows a class attribute keeps the constant role, with the instance's value.
  • Array attributes. Their dtype, full shape and vector width.
  • Runtime scalar names. Instance scalars are runtime parameters, so their values are not keyed. Their names are, because adding or removing one changes the parameter layout.

Note

Template array attributes are keyed by their full shape, which is stricter than plain array arguments (those specialize only on the dimensions in the shape signature). Changing the length of a template's array therefore lowers a new IR template and compiles a new variant even when no dimension is baked in. This over-specializes, which is safe; it is a cost, not a correctness issue.

docs.title: shape_sig: dimensions baked into code
docs.text:
resolve_ir substitutes array dimensions as literals: a[i, j] becomes i * 8 + j when a.shape[1] == 8. That literal is part of the compiled code's identity. shape_signature(template, name_to_array) reports exactly the dimensions a kernel bakes in, as a tuple of concrete sizes.

It is built from ir_shape_deps(ir_func), which scans the template once and memoizes the result on it as _shape_deps (it depends on the source, not on the arguments):

  • _dependent_nodes yields every node whose value reaches generated code, skipping the parallel loop's end.
  • Each IRDimSize(array, d) contributes (array, d). The array name is mapped through _static_array_aliases, which follows the __<func>_<param>_<N>__ = param copies that @tack.func inlining creates.
  • Each IRTextureSample contributes all three dimensions of its texture.

shape_signature then looks up each (name, d) in this call's arguments, using shape_3d for textures, _logical_shape for vector arrays and shape otherwise. A kernel with no baked-in dimensions gets the empty tuple, so the common 1-D kernel pays nothing for shape keying.

Why the parallel loop's end is excluded. It never reaches generated code. Code generators read it from the __loop_end__ parameter, and _get_loop_range evaluates it against the arguments on every dispatch. resolve_ir leaves it unresolved for the same reason. Without the exclusion, for i in range(x.shape[0]), the most common line in any kernel, would compile a new variant for every array length.

Kernel line Baked-in dimensions for i in range(x.shape[0]): out[i] = x[i] * 2 none for i in range(1, x.shape[0] - 1): …x[i-1] + x[i+1]… none (the start moves into the body as a constant) out[i] = x[x.shape[0] - 1 - i] x.shape[0] for i, j in tack.ndindex(a.shape[0], a.shape[1]): out[i, j] = a[i, j] a.shape[1], out.shape[1] (the row count only sets the launch) v = tex.sample(u, v, w) all three extents of tex

docs.title: disjoint: the CPU no-overlap bit
docs.text:
Arrays may share storage: the same array passed twice, two views of one allocation, or imported pointers. Generated code therefore never promises noalias/restrict unconditionally (contract regression LC2; see Memory and Aliasing). Without that promise, though, LLVM must reload after every store and cannot vectorize a loop that accumulates through an array.

The CPU backend recovers that case with a second variant. It calls resolve_variant(..., specialize_disjoint=True) (the module constant _SPECIALIZE_DISJOINT in runtime/cpu.py), and on every dispatch arrays_disjoint(template, effective_args) decides whether this call qualifies:

  1. written_array_params(template) finds the array parameters the kernel may store to, directly, atomically, or through @tack.func pointer copies, by a fixed point over name copies. If a store goes through a name it cannot trace back to a parameter or a local allocation, it returns None and every array counts as written. The result, and a per-parameter flag tuple, are memoized on the template.
  2. Each array argument's byte range comes from its buffer's span (NumpyBuffer.span, cached per array). A buffer without a span makes the answer False.
  3. The call qualifies when no written range overlaps any other array's range. Read-only arrays may overlap each other freely: dot(x, x) still qualifies.

The answer is the last key element and is stored on the variant's IR as disjoint_arrays. LLVMCodeGen then adds noalias to array parameters only in that variant. Both variants must agree on every race-free program, so overlapping and non-overlapping calls of one kernel each get correct code; a kernel that is sometimes called with aliased arrays simply has two variants. GPU backends never pass specialize_disjoint, so for them the element is always False.

The check costs a little on every CPU dispatch. Whether that pays for itself depends on the host and the kernel; the tradeoff is discussed in Memory and Aliasing.

docs.title: What is deliberately not in the key
docs.text: Not keyed Why that is safe Scalar argument values (within one inferred type) scalars are runtime parameters; on GPU they are rewritten into the pack buffers on each dispatch The outer launch length read from __loop_end__, evaluated per dispatch Template instance scalar values runtime parameters; only their names are keyed Array contents and addresses never baked in; the only address-derived fact is the CPU disjoint bit The kernel's name each Kernel object has its own cache slot The backend each backend instance has its own cache Debug mode, as a flag not needed: a debug template has two more parameters, so its param_sig differs; the IR template key and the disk keys name it A floating-point math mode there is one fixed policy (see Numerical Semantics); a selectable mode would have to join the key Device-function bindings consulted only when an IR template is built; rebinding afterwards is unsupported, so recreate the kernel. The disk cache does record them (below)

docs.title: Cache structure and lifetime
docs.text:
Each backend creates its cache in __init__ with new_kernel_cache():

backend._cache: WeakKeyDictionary[Kernel, dict[variant_key, KernelVariant]]

kernel_cache_slot(cache, kernel) returns, or creates, the kernel's inner dictionary.

Keyed on the Kernel object, held weakly. An earlier cache was keyed on id(kernel). A garbage-collected kernel frees its address, and a new kernel allocated there with the same name and argument types silently ran the old kernel's code. Keying on the object removes that hazard, and holding it weakly releases compiled code and its device modules when the kernel goes away. Most kernels are module-level objects that live as long as the process, and so do their variants.

One cache per backend instance. Each device is one backend with its own cache. tack.device(spec) without options returns the same backend every time, so switching the default device away and back keeps its compiled variants, and arrays made before a switch run on their own device with its variants. A device made with options (tack.device("cpu", num_threads=1)) is a new backend with a new, empty cache.

Every cache is registered. new_kernel_cache appends a weak reference to the module-level _kernel_caches list. drop_variants(kernel, is_stale) walks every live cache, not only the default device's, which matters for template-class retirement.

docs.title: Template-class lifetime: _ClassToken
docs.text:
Keying a variant on a template class object would keep the class alive as long as the kernel. A class defined inside a function and created on every call would then leave one IR template and one variant behind per call, forever. Instead, lang/kernel.py keys on a _ClassToken:

  • _class_token(cls) returns the class's token from _class_tokens, a WeakKeyDictionary from class to token, creating it on first use and registering weakref.finalize(cls, _retire_class, token).
  • Each token records the kernels specialized on it (token.kernels, a WeakSet).
  • When the class is collected, _retire_class removes every IR template in those kernels' _ir_cache whose key names the token, and calls drop_variants to remove every variant whose template key (the third key element) names it, in every live backend cache.

The token provides identity without a strong reference: distinct classes never share a variant, and a collected class takes its specializations with it.

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text:
The warm path takes no lock: the IR template lookup and the variant lookup are dictionary reads.

  • IR templates are built under _transform_lock with a re-check, so a template is lowered once even when several threads miss together.
  • Key derivation writes argument types onto a per-dispatch _KeyProbe rather than the shared template, so concurrent dispatches with different dtypes cannot read each other's annotations.
  • Variant construction is not locked. Two threads that miss on the same key both build. kernel_cache_slot uses setdefault, so neither replaces the other's slot dictionary, and the second slot[key] = variant overwrites the first. Each thread returns the variant it built, and both are correct, so the only cost is a duplicate compile.
  • Launching a variant is serialized where a variant owns launch state. On CUDA and HIP that is the pack buffers its scalars are written into, and they hold the variant's dispatch_lock (a slot of KernelVariant) from the pack update until the launch is queued, so dispatches of different variants still overlap. Level Zero holds one backend-wide _launch_lock, because its command list and kernel argument state are shared by the whole backend. Metal's launches own their argument buffer and scalars and encode under the backend's batch lock. The CPU binds arguments per call and takes no lock, though its JIT'd pool runs one fan-out at a time. See Backend Implementations.
  • The fast path's entries are plain dictionary writes; the slot is cleared when it reaches its cap of 256 signatures per kernel and backend.

docs.title: Hit versus miss
docs.text:
Step Hit Miss classify arguments (templates, vectors, textures) ✓ ✓ IR template lookup (a template key is built for template/vector/texture calls) ✓ ✓ check_workgroup_support (memoized on the template on the CPU, immediate on GPU) ✓ ✓ type inference on the _KeyProbe, shape_signature, arrays_disjoint (CPU) ✓ ✓ build the key, look up the variant ✓ ✓ look up the variant in the disk cache, and load it on a disk hit ✓ clone_ir, resolve, infer, check, localize, atomic/workgroup analysis, optimize (on a disk miss) ✓ verify_ir at each boundary ✓ GPU clone and scalar packing, annotate_types, codegen, native compile ✓ check_workgroup_launch (collective kernels), check_atomic_alignment, check_writable_arrays ✓ ✓ evaluate the launch range, check_launch_size (GPU), update pack buffers and queue the launch under the variant's lock (CUDA, HIP) ✓ ✓

A hit clones nothing, runs no passes and performs no verification. The memoized template facts (_shape_deps, _written_flags, _workgroup_features) and the variant's recorded atomic_targets and written_arrays keep the remaining per-dispatch work proportional to the parameter count rather than to the kernel's size.

docs.title: The dispatch fast path
docs.text:
Even a hit walked the arguments half a dozen times: template detection and expansion, vector and texture detection, the IR lookup, type inference on the probe, the shape signature, the key. Each took a few microseconds, and together they were the largest part of a dispatch's host time (90 of about 270 µs per launch of a contour's kernels on a 2 GHz Xeon). So resolve_variant first tries _fast_resolve: a call whose signature was seen before reuses what that call resolved.

The signature (_call_signature) is read straight off the arguments: an array's dtype, shape and element layout (memoized on the array as _sig); a texture's extents; a scalar's kind and, for integers, the type its value selects; a template object's class token, its class constants' current values, and what the key and the expansion read of each attribute, nested templates by path. Equal signatures imply an equal variant key, so an entry, kept per backend and kernel, holds the expansion plan for template arguments, the variants it resolved by disjointness, and the array slots for the overlap check. A hit expands the templates through the plan, decides disjointness, runs the per-call checks (_check_call: full workgroups, atomic alignment, read-only arrays) and returns. Entries hold no class, and drop_variants forgets the kernel's entries on every backend along with its variants, so a per-call template class is still collected and a dropped variant is resolved afresh. A call with keyword arguments, an argument the signature cannot describe, or debug mode (its variants take hidden arguments, and each launch is noted for the check) takes the slow path. Together with the CPU passing array addresses rather than typed pointer objects, a warm CPU dispatch went from 70 to 40 µs.

docs.title: What a warm call costs
docs.text: What a warm call pays (_fast_resolve): the call's signature (_call_signature, cached per Array as _sig; per template class the attribute layout _template_layouts, relearned when an instance's attribute names or types differ), one weak lookup for the kernel's entry, the disjointness check over the entry's precomputed array slots (_disjoint_by_slots, one sorted walk), and the per-call checks. It runs outside template_scope, which the slow path enters. NumpyBuffer.address and span are computed once per array. Measured on a 2 GHz Xeon: a warm CPU dispatch 70 → 40 µs from the signature alone, then a serial dispatch with eight array arguments 66 → 34 µs; inside a filter, where launches follow cache-trashing kernels and a third are template views, 149 → 130 µs per launch. Leaving the caller out of the chunks (k workers, caller waits) was tried for its warm caches and lost (161 µs), so the caller still runs chunks.

docs.title: The correctness argument
docs.text:
The design rests on one rule: anything a pass or code generator bakes into the compiled code must be named by the key. Leaving something out causes silent wrong numbers, while keying too much only costs compile time. The table pairs each baked-in fact with the key element that names it:

Baked into the variant By Named by parameter types, expression types, pack layout inference, annotation, packing param_sig[*].type_annotation pointer versus value calling convention codegen, packing param_sig[*]._is_array sampler versus software sampling, texture extents codegen, store_texture_shapes param_sig[*]._is_texture, _texture_shape, shape_sig vector scalarization AST transform vec_sig (and the IR template key) inlined template methods, class constants, template parameter layout template rewrite tmpl_key dimension literals in index arithmetic and loops resolve_ir shape_sig noalias on array pointers LLVMCodeGen disjoint everything derived from the source all stages the per-kernel slot

This rule has been learned the hard way. The cache was once keyed on id(kernel) (reused addresses ran another kernel's code); then on types alone (a new row stride reused code with the old stride baked in); then without vector widths (LC3). Each was a silent wrong-numbers bug. The regression tests for this area are in packages/tack-core/tests/test_variant_cache.py, test_kernel_cache.py, test_array_shape.py and test_disjoint_arrays.py.

docs.title: Worked examples
docs.text:
The variant counts below were observed on the CPU backend at this release by inspecting backend._cache[kernel] after each call, starting from an empty cache. All arrays are f32 unless noted. The disjoint bit is True for every call except the aliased one.

@tack.kernel
def scale(x, out, a):
    for i in range(x.shape[0]):
        out[i] = x[i] * a
Call Variants Why scale(x8, o8, 2.0), then lengths 16 and 32 1 the only dimension is the launch bound scale(x8, o8, 3.5) 1 a new scalar value is a runtime argument scale(x8, o8, 3) 2 int infers i32, not f32 scale(x8, o8, 2**40) 3 beyond the i32 range, so i64 scale(x8_f64, o8_f64, 2.0) 4 new array dtype, and the float scalar becomes f64 scale(x, x, 2.0) 5 the written array overlaps another array, so the disjoint bit is False Kernel Calls Variants out[i] = x[x.shape[0] - 1 - i] lengths 8, 16, 32 3 the same with n passed as a scalar: out[i] = x[n - 1 - i] lengths 8, 16, 32 1 tack.ndindex(a.shape[0], a.shape[1]) over 2-D arrays shapes (4, 8), (16, 8), (4, 9) 2 range(1, x.shape[0] - 1) stencil lengths 8, 16, 32 1 out[i] = v[i].dot(v[i]) with tack.Array with a vector element dtype widths 2, then 3 2 (and 2 IR templates)

For a @tack.device_class class with a class constant factor, an instance scalar offset and an instance array data:

Call Variants IR templates Why first call 1 1 new offset value 1 1 instance scalars are runtime parameters data of a different length 2 2 template array shapes are keyed s.factor = 3.0 on the instance 3 3 it shadows a class constant, so it stays a constant an equivalent class defined inside a function 4 4 different class identity ... after that class is garbage-collected 3 3 _retire_class dropped its specializations

docs.title: The disk cache
docs.text:
runtime/disk_cache.py keeps both kinds of cached code across processes. The in-memory caches above stay in front of it: the disk is consulted only on an in-memory miss, so a warm dispatch never touches it. User-facing settings are on The Kernel Cache.

Why the front end is cached too. A cold contour of a 21³ grid on an M1 Max spent about 1.15 s in 18 new kernels: 0.46 s lowering (template rewriting included), about 0.25 s in the IR passes and the verifier, 0.19 s generating MSL and 0.21 s in Metal's compiler. A cache of binaries alone would save the smallest part.

Two levels.

Entry Key Holds .ir the kernel's module, qualified name and source; its result type; its closure cells' fingerprints; vector and texture arrays; each template's content; whether debug mode lowered it; Tack's fingerprint the pickled IRModule, and the names lowering resolved .variant the .ir entry's key and dependency digest; parameter types and categories, texture shapes, vector widths, shape_sig, disjoint; the backend and Backend.cache_target() the post-pass IR, requires_full_workgroups, the atomic targets, and the backend's artifact

Debug mode is in the .ir key, and the .variant key follows from the .ir entry, so a debug kernel and a plain one never share an entry in either direction: without it, a debug process read the plain kernel from disk and its launch, missing the hidden arguments, failed. A debug kernel read from disk still names the access it caught, because its sites travel in the IR.

A template's content replaces the identities of the in-memory key: each class by its method resolution order (module and qualified name), its @tack.func methods by source and __tack_iterate__; device functions held as attributes by source; constants by value (floats by bit pattern).

Names lowering resolved. The in-memory IR cache relies on the documented rule that bindings do not change during a process. Across processes they do: a device function is edited, a constant changes. Every CallBindings.resolve during a lowering is recorded (_Recorder) as the owner function, the dotted name, and a fingerprint of what it resolved to: a Func by its source, a tack.constant by value, a module by name, and "unbound" for a bare intrinsic. On a read, each name is resolved again in the current owner (_lookup, which follows CallBindings' rules) and the entry is used only if every fingerprint matches. Owners are the kernel, its templates' methods and function attributes, and each device function a recorded name resolved to, in recording order. A name bound to an object with no stable fingerprint, or a lowering with an explicit bindings namespace, is not stored. The closure cells are in the key itself, so kernels a factory makes over different device functions keep separate entries instead of replacing each other on every run.

Tack's fingerprint covers everything else lowering and code generation depend on: the RECORD of each installed Tack package (one read each), or every source file of a source tree on the path (editable installs: 167 files, 16 ms, once per process), plus the format version and Python's minor version. It names the directory the entries live in, so another Tack never reads them.

Artifacts. Backend.cache_target(), variant_artifact(payload) and load_variant(ir_func, artifact, effective_args); a backend whose cache_target() is None stores only the .ir level; every backend stores variants now. effective_args are the call's arguments: a GPU variant's scalar pack buffers are device memory of the process, so a load makes them anew from the call's scalars, as _build_variant does.

Backend Artifact Loading it CPU the object code MCJIT emitted (set_object_cache) add_object_file into a new engine: about 0.4 ms, no LLVM optimization or code generation Metal MSL source, entry name, parameter layout, scalar pack layout newLibraryWithSource, which macOS's own shader cache makes fast for source it has compiled before CUDA PTX from NVRTC, entry name, parameter layout, scalar pack layout cuModuleLoadData: the driver compiles the PTX for the device, so the target names the device and compute capability, the driver version, NVRTC's version and its options HIP the code object from hipRTC, entry name, parameter layout, scalar pack layout hipModuleLoadData: machine code for one architecture, so the target names the device and gcnArchName with its feature flags (which also separates devices with and without texture hardware), the ROCm runtime and driver, hipRTC, hip-python and the hipRTC options Level Zero the native binary IGC made (zeModuleGetNativeBinary), the SPIR-V from ocloc, entry name, parameter layout, workgroup size, scalar pack layout zeModuleCreate in the backend's context (its own or the adopted one) as ZE_MODULE_FORMAT_NATIVE: about 0.2 ms a kernel. A binary the driver refuses loads from the SPIR-V, which IGC finalizes, about 50 ms a kernel without the driver's own cache. The target names the device and its IP version (stepping), the driver version, ocloc's version, the ocloc and module options, and f64 support

File-system rules. Entries are written to a temporary file in the same directory and renamed into place, atomic on POSIX file systems including Lustre and GPFS; concurrent writers of one entry write the same bytes. No locks. Each entry starts with a magic string and a SHA-256 of its payload, and holds its own key; anything else is ignored and counted as bad. The directory and the per-version directory must belong to the user and be writable by nobody else, since loading an entry unpickles it; the cache creates both with mode 0700, since under a umask of 002 a directory it made itself was group-writable and then refused. The entries of every Tack version share one size limit (TACK_CACHE_SIZE, 1 GiB by default): past it, a writing process deletes the least recently used entries until 90% of the limit is left, scanning the directory at most once an hour across processes (a .pruned mark), never per kernel; a hit refreshes its entry's time at most once an hour, and bundles are neither counted nor deleted. Under MPI (a launcher's rank variable with a world size above one) the default mode is bundle: one file per Tack version, read once per process (or by rank 0 and broadcast, load_bundle(comm=...)), and no per-kernel file is looked up or written. In write mode under MPI only rank 0 stores. Nothing compiles collectively: ranks reach different kernels, so a collective there could deadlock.

conftest.py sets TACK_CACHE=off unless the environment chooses, so the suite compiles from scratch; test_disk_cache.py runs its cases in fresh processes against a temporary directory. TACK_CACHE=write pytest, run twice, serves most of the second run from disk.

docs.title: Costs and advice
docs.text:
Variants multiply: every distinct combination of dtypes, scalar types, vector widths, baked-in dimensions, template constants and (on the CPU) aliasing produces its own compile. Each cold compile pays for cloning, the pass pipeline, verification at every boundary, code generation and the native compiler. The first call of a large kernel is noticeably slower than a warm one, and a workload that keeps producing new variants never reaches the warm path.

To keep the number of variants down:

  • Pass lengths as scalars when a dimension would otherwise appear inside the body. def reverse(x, out, n) compiles once; reading x.shape[0] in the index compiles once per length. Dimensions that appear only in the outermost range never specialize.
  • Keep scalar types stable. Integer scalars are typed by value: a value that crosses the i32 range selects a new i64 variant. Float scalars follow the precision of the array arguments.
  • Use instance attributes for values that change, class attributes for true constants. Class constants are baked in, and each new value compiles a new variant.
  • Define @tack.device_class classes once, at module level. A class defined per call is a new identity each time. Its variants are released when it is collected, but each call still pays a cold compile.
  • Expect re-specialization when a template's array changes shape. Its full shape is part of the template key.

Specializing on baked-in dimensions is usually worth it: a known row stride lets LLVM and the vendor compilers fold and vectorize around it. The advice above is for the cases where the set of shapes is open-ended.

docs.title: Vendor workarounds
docs.text:
Tack generates source for five toolchains and calls four vendor runtimes through bindings, and some of what it emits is shaped around a defect in one of them rather than by the language contract. This page lists each such workaround with the vendor and version it was found on, what goes wrong without it, where it lives, and the test that would notice if it were removed. The point is to know when one can go: a workaround guards a version range, and a driver fix makes it dead weight that still costs something (a function call, a slower path, a missed optimization).

To retire one, run its test on the newest toolchain with the workaround switched off. If the test passes there and on the oldest version Tack still supports, remove it and record the versions here.

Design choices that look like workarounds but are not are listed at the end: they follow from the contract, and no vendor fix would remove them.

docs.title: Metal (Apple)
docs.text: Workaround Found on Without it Where Test A kernel whose sequential loop stores to an array (or runs an atomic) has its body in a noinline function, __tack_body__, that the entry calls; workgroup arrays are declared in the entry and passed as pointers. M1 Max, Apple's GPU back end at pipeline creation (2026) Wrong results: the compiler read an array element once before the loop when its address did not depend on the thread and the loop stored to another array of the same type (total[0] += x[k]; counter[0] += 1). The front end's LLVM IR is correct; alias metadata is not the cause, and restrict, opaque pointers and compile options do not avoid it. msl_gen._stores_inside_sequential_loop, _BODY_FUNCTION test_array_updates_in_loops.py i64/u64 additions that update an accumulator inside a runtime-bound loop go through separate noinline helpers. M1 Max compiler The Metal compiler crashed. msl_gen (_opaque_integer_add), codegen/integer_ops.py none dedicated; i64 accumulator loops on Metal would crash the compiler again A typed or integer constant array read at a runtime index is one constant table (IRTableLoad), not a select chain. Metal's compiler service Select chains inside a storing loop crashed the compiler service. codegen/tables.py, ast_transform (constant_table) test_constant_tables.py Every new... selector Tack calls is registered as returning an owned object (_OWNED_RESULTS) before any is called. pyobjc-framework-Metal 12.1 Its metadata omits already_retained, so PyObjC retained each buffer, texture, library and pipeline once more and none was ever freed; a benchmark's temporaries reached 150 GB. runtime/metal.py test_arrays_own_their_buffers_alone in test_metal.py

docs.title: CUDA (NVIDIA)
docs.text:
Workaround Found on Without it Where Test i8/i16 negation and abs go through an inline-PTX sub.u32 (__tack_ptx_neg_u32__). H100, driver 595.58 (CUDA 13.2): ptxas 12.0-13.2 and the PTX JIT of drivers before 13.3, on sm_80, sm_89 and sm_90 alike PTX neg.s16/abs.s16 were widened without re-extending, so the wrapped minimum came back as its magnitude. codegen/integer_ops.py (_negates_in_ptx), _ptx_negation in cuda_gen.py test_narrow_negation_avoids_ptx_neg_s16 (test_cuda.py) checks the PTX, since drivers from 13.3 pass the widening test either way

docs.title: HIP (AMD)
docs.text:
Workaround Found on Without it Where Test hiprtcDestroyProgram is never called (a small leak, bounded by kernel caching). hip-python 7.1; still crashing on hip-python 7.2.2 with ROCm 7.0.2 (MI300X, 2026-08-11) SIGSEGV on the first call, after a successful compile. The documented convention (hiprtcDestroyProgram(prog)) is the one that crashes; a pointer to the program is refused as a type error. runtime/hip_backend.py none: removing it crashes the process hipRTC compiles with -ffp-contract=on (_HIPRTC_OPTIONS). hipRTC's default fast contraction A product was fused into one read of a variable while another read of it stayed rounded, so a - a != 0.0 was true for finite a (the finiteness test in _crossing). runtime/hip_backend.py none dedicated; the dataset contour tests on HIP failed without it (_crossing in tack.dataset.algorithms._common) Waits go through ctypes on the runtime library (_runtime, _StreamMarker), never hip-python's hipStreamSynchronize. hip-python 7.x wrappers; ROCm 7.1 hip-python holds the GIL while the runtime waits (another thread ran 6 times during a 357 ms wait, 353 through ctypes), and ROCm 7.1's stream synchronize holds the stream, so another thread's launch waited the whole 350 ms. runtime/hip_backend.py test_hip_async.py, test_asyncio.py HIPTextureImage writes array handles and fixed-size arrays through ctypes, located from neighbouring views. hip-python 7.x struct wrappers make_hipExtent and friends are gone, hipCreateChannelDesc returns (err, desc), nested members are read-only views, and res.array.array, hipMemcpy3DParms.dstArray and hipTextureDesc.addressMode are not exposed at all. runtime/hip_backend.py test_hip.py (texture tests; MI210 with point filtering) Textures fall back to software sampling where the device has no image hardware, and on gfx90a. MI300 (gfx940-942) has no texture hardware; gfx90a (MI200) reports image support but refuses a linearly filtered 3D texture (hipErrorNotSupported) hipRTC refuses tex3D ("The image/texture API not supported on the device"), or texture creation fails. HIPBackend.texture_in_hardware (asks hipDeviceAttributeImageSupport and tries a 2×2×2 texture at init) test_texture_snapshot.py A launch is capped below 2^32 work-items. AMD's dispatch packet The packet counts work-items in 32 bits; a larger grid would wrap. HIPBackend._query_max_launch test_launch_limits.py

A known defect left in place. ROCm 7.0.2 and 7.1.1's device compiler (AMD clang 20, in hipRTC's comgr) miscompiles one generated integer expression at -O1 and above (a 64-bit signed -253 < -1 inside the full expression evaluates false). It depends on the surrounding expression, so Tack does not try to avoid it; test_integer_expression_differential.py marks that case as a strict expected failure when hipRuntimeGetVersion() reports ROCm 7.0 or 7.1, and a fixed toolchain reports XPASS, when the mark goes. Details in Backend implementations.

hip-python 10 is a compatibility package over rocm.bindings that moved several names (LONG_VERSION, hip.chip, output structs, string fields); hip_backend.py supports both. That is an API change rather than a defect, and goes when 7.x support does.

docs.text: Workaround Found on Without it Where Test Signed negation below 32 bits and abs below 64 are noinline helpers. IGC 2.7.11 (compute runtime 25.05, Max 1100) The wrapped minimum was widened as its magnitude: i16 -(-32768) came back as 32768. codegen/integer_ops.py, opencl_gen.py test_opencl_gen.py (test_widenable_negation_and_abs_are_noinline), test_integer_semantics.py (test_wrapped_negation_and_abs_survive_widening) on Level Zero The global index is built from get_group_id(0), widened, times the group size, not from get_global_id(0). Driver 25.05 In-order lists (ZE_COMMAND_QUEUE_FLAG_IN_ORDER) cost about 100 µs of device time per kernel; a barrier costs about 5. level_zero_backend._ordered test_level_zero_async.py Copies to the device up to 16 MiB and from it up to 64 KiB go through pooled USM host memory (_HostStaging). Driver 25.05 Appending a copy from pageable memory did not return until the queue drained (to the device up to 4 MiB, from it up to 1 KiB), so a launch's scalar upload waited for every kernel before it. level_zero_backend.py test_level_zero_async.py f64 floor and ceil are wrapped as copysign(floor(x), x). Max 1100, intel-opencl-icd 25.05.32567.17 The double overloads returned +0.0 for ceil(-0.1) and floor(-0.0), where IEEE 754 requires -0.0; the f32 overloads are correct. Exact for every input, since neither function changes its operand's sign. OpenCLCodeGen._expr_call test_float_semantics.py on Level Zero A stored native binary the driver refuses is rebuilt from the stored SPIR-V. Drivers that refuse another build's native binary The disk cache entry would be unusable. Counted as native_refused in the cache stats. level_zero_backend.load_variant test_disk_cache.py (test_a_refused_native_binary_falls_back_to_spirv)

docs.title: CPU (LLVM)
docs.text: Workaround Found on Without it Where Test The native assembly parser is initialized before the thread pool is built. llvmlite on Apple silicon The pool program uses inline asm (yield); without the parser LLVM aborts the process instead of raising. runtime/cpu_pool.py (_target_machine) test_cpu_pool.py

docs.title: Not workarounds
docs.text:
These shape generated code or runtime behavior for reasons in the language contract or in Tack's own design; no vendor fix would remove them.

  • Metal array arguments are members of one argument buffer: separate device-buffer arguments promise disjoint storage in MSL, and arrays may alias (docs/design/memory-and-aliasing.md).
  • CUDA/HIP widen blockIdx.x before multiplying by blockDim.x, because the built-ins are 32-bit; this is C's arithmetic, not a defect.
  • Precise floating options (no --use_fast_math, fastMathEnabled off) are the floating-point contract.
  • Level Zero refuses arrays from another context because Intel's driver resolves pointers from any context, so Tack's check is the only one (test_level_zero_context.py).
  • Integer helpers for floor division, remainder, wrapping and power exist on every GPU backend because C leaves those cases undefined or different.
  • Two CUDA spellings that OpenCL C forbids are rewritten for Level Zero: a floating condition in ?: (_ifexp_condition compares it against zero) and __local declarations in nested scopes (_declare_local hoists them to the kernel's outermost scope). These are the dialect's rules.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
The longer history of the narrowest ones, kept from the backend notes.

HIP: hiprtcDestroyProgram is never called. In hip-python it segfaults on the first call after a successful compile. Recorded against 7.1 and confirmed again on 2026-08-11 with hip-python 7.2.2 on ROCm 7.0.2 (MI300X). The documented calling convention is the one that crashes. Tack skips the call in _compile_code_object; each compile leaks one program object, which the variant cache keeps rare.

Metal: an opaque 64-bit add in one loop shape. On an M1 Max, pipeline compilation crashed when a wrapping 64-bit addition took part in reduction optimization inside a loop with a runtime bound. MSLCodeGen._emit_assign sets _opaque_integer_add while emitting an assignment whose value reads its own target, inside a sequential loop whose end is not a constant; _expr_binop then emits that i64/u64 + through a helper declared __attribute__((noinline)) (IntegerCodeGen in codegen/integer_ops.py). Every other integer operation stays inline.

Level Zero: opaque signed negation and abs. On an Intel Data Center GPU Max 1100 (IGC 2.7.11), a wrapped negation or abs of a signed minimum was correct at its own width but lost its sign when widened: i16 -(-32768) stored to an i32 array read 32768, and abs of the i8, i16 and i32 minimum widened as its magnitude. The SPIR-V from ocloc was correct, -ze-opt-disable hid the error, and no inlined form tried — as_short, a select on the minimum, complement-plus-one, a sign mask — survived the driver's folding; LLVM canonicalizes them all to the same shape. OpenCLCodeGen sets _opaque_negation, and IntegerCodeGen emits neg below 32 bits and abs below 64 bits as __attribute__((noinline)) helpers. i32 negation, i64 abs and every other operation stay inline. test_wrapped_negation_and_abs_survive_widening covers the widened results on each backend.

CUDA: signed negation and abs below 32 bits as inline PTX. On an H100 with driver 595.58 (CUDA 13.2), the same symptom: i16 -(-32768) and abs(-32768) widened as 32768. Tack's C and NVRTC's PTX are correct (neg.s16, then cvt.s64.s16); the driver's JIT is not. ptxas 12.0 through 13.2 sign-extend the input, negate in 32 bits and widen that without re-extending from bit 15; ptxas 13.3 does not, and the architecture does not matter (sm_80, sm_89 and sm_90 alike). Only neg.s16 and abs.s16 are affected. NVVM narrows every C spelling of the negation to those instructions, so CUDACodeGen sets _ptx_negation and IntegerCodeGen negates i8 and i16 (for neg and abs) with __tack_ptx_neg_u32__, an inline-PTX sub.u32 on the 32-bit carrier, then narrows as before. A noinline helper also gave the right answer, but only because its caller re-extended the returned short. HIP and OpenCL inherit CUDACodeGen and turn the option off. test_narrow_negation_avoids_ptx_neg_s16 checks the PTX, since drivers from 13.3 pass the widening test either way.

Level Zero: f64 floor and ceil lose the sign of zero. On an Intel Data Center GPU Max 1100 (intel-opencl-icd 25.05.32567.17), the double overloads returned +0.0 for ceil(-0.1) and floor(-0.0), where IEEE 754 requires -0.0. The f32 overloads are correct. OpenCLCodeGen._expr_call wraps those two builtins at double width as copysign(floor(x), x). Neither function ever changes the sign of its operand, so restoring it is exact for every input, and a no-op where the runtime is already correct.

OpenCL C dialect rules. Two inherited CUDA spellings are illegal OpenCL C and failed only on the device: a floating-point condition in ?: (_ifexp_condition compares it against zero), and __local declarations in nested scopes (_declare_local hoists them to the kernel's outermost scope, which is legal because local memory is per-workgroup and statically sized).

CUDA exports avoid Win32 NT handles. _EXPORT_HANDLE_TYPES uses CU_MEM_HANDLE_TYPE_WIN32_KMT on Windows. On a GeForce RTX 5060 the NT handle type was refused by cuMemCreate despite the device attribute claiming support, and cuda-python 13.3.1 segfaulted when asked for it with security attributes; _create_backing therefore trusts a successful allocation, not the attribute.

docs.title: Tack Developer's Guide
docs.text:
This guide explains Tack's internals for contributors and anyone who wants to understand how Python kernel source becomes GPU machine code.

This guide is task-oriented: how the pieces are laid out and how to change them. Two other sections go deeper:

  • Design and Implementation explains why each part is built the way it is and how it works end to end: the compilation pipeline, specialization and caching, numerical semantics, parallel execution, memory and aliasing, the CPU threading policy, each backend, and interoperability.
  • Contracts states what is guaranteed: the kernel language contract (draft), the backend capability and runtime API contracts, and how conformance is tested.

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
1. Architecture Overview — Compilation pipeline, module layout
  2. AST Transform — Python AST to Tack IR
  3. IR Design — Node types, structure, invariants
  4. IR Passes — Resolve, optimize, type annotate, scalar packing
  5. Codegen — LLVM, MSL, CUDA, HIP, OpenCL
  6. Runtime and Dispatch — Backend lifecycle, array allocation, kernel dispatch
  7. Template System — @tack.device_class, template rewrite, @tack.func inlining
  8. Adding a New Feature — Walkthrough of adding a new IR node

docs.title: Host compiler checks
docs.text:
Several codegen tests compile OpenCL C or run generated C++ on the host, including checks with undefined-behavior sanitization. They complement the vendor compiler and hardware tests; they do not require a GPU.

All these checks share compiler discovery and preflight. Set TACK_CLANG to a Clang executable outside PATH if needed. C++ checks use its adjacent clang++ (including a version suffix); set TACK_CLANGXX explicitly for a wrapper or a different C++ driver. An invalid explicit choice fails rather than falling back to another compiler. Without overrides, discovery tries unversioned drivers on PATH, followed by versioned drivers.

Developer runs may skip missing or unusable default tooling with a reason. Set TACK_REQUIRE_CLANG=1 for validation: absent compilers, missing headers, and missing UBSan link/runtime support then fail. The Linux and Metal CI suite jobs require these checks and run their preflight before the suite.

export TACK_CLANG=/absolute/path/to/clang
export TACK_REQUIRE_CLANG=1
uv run pytest -q -s packages/tack-core/tests/test_compiler_tools.py \
  -k test_host_compiler_preflight

Preflight compiles OpenCL C 2.0 and C++17, then links and executes a small UBSan-instrumented program. Select an installation with its headers and sanitizer runtimes, and supply any required library/SDK paths in the same environment as the suite. Compiler preflight is cached per driver and execution environment; each generated kernel is still compiled by its test.

docs.title: Compilation Pipeline
docs.text:
When a @tack.kernel is called, every backend's execute() goes through resolve_variant() in runtime/kernel_utils.py, which runs this pipeline:

@tack.kernel Python function
  Once per IR template (vector widths, texture extents, template structure,
  debug mode), unless the disk cache has it:              [disk_cache.py]
    → Template rewrite (if @tack.device_class args)     [template_rewrite.py]
    → Source validation (reject unsupported syntax)      [source_validation.py]
    → AST transform → Tack IR, @tack.func inlining       [ast_transform.py, lowering/, call_bindings.py]
      (debug mode: bounds checks on every index)         [ir_bounds.py]
    → Verify 'lowered', cache the template on the Kernel [ir_verify.py, kernel.py]
  Once per compiled variant (cache miss), on a clone_ir copy of the template,
  unless the disk cache has it:
    → IR resolve (dimension sizes, texture shapes)       [ir_resolve.py]
    → Type inference (from actual arguments)             [type_inference.py]
    → Dispatch type check (backend dtypes)               [type_inference.py]
    → Scalar localization (params and outer locals)      [kernel_utils.py]
    → Atomic / workgroup checks                          [atomic_support.py, workgroup_*.py]
    → IR optimize (conservative copy propagation)        [ir_optimize.py]
    → Scalar packing (GPU backends only, on a copy)      [ir_pack_scalars.py]
    → IR type annotate (resolved types for codegen)      [ir_type_annotate.py]
      (debug mode: guard checked accesses)               [ir_bounds.py]
    → Backend-specific codegen + native compile, store on disk
  Every call:
    → Read the call's signature; a known one reuses its variant (fast path)
    → Otherwise derive the variant key, look it up
    → Alignment, read-only and launch-size checks        [kernel_utils.py]
    → Bind texture storage and arguments, launch (queued on GPU backends)
    → Debug mode: raise IndexError for an out-of-bounds access [debug_bounds.py]

verify_ir() checks the IR after each of these stages. The IR template cached on the Kernel is never mutated; each new variant clones it and the passes mutate the clone. Compiled variants are cached per backend and per kernel object, under a key built from argument dtypes and array/scalar/texture categories, vector widths, texture extents, template structure and constants, the dimension sizes baked into the code, and (on the CPU) whether the array arguments overlap. A repeat call with the same key runs no passes and no verification; a repeat call with the same argument signature does not even build the key. Lowered templates and compiled variants are also kept on disk, keyed by content, so a new process can skip both. See Compilation Pipeline and Specialization and Caching for the full account.

docs.title: Package Structure
docs.text:
Tack is split into two packages in a monorepo:

packages/
    tack-core/                    # Core compute framework
        src/tack/
            __init__.py          # Public API + pkgutil.extend_path
            lang/                # Frontend: AST → IR
                kernel.py        # @tack.kernel decorator, Kernel class, IR template cache
                func.py          # @tack.func decorator, Func class
                device_class.py  # @tack.device_class decorator
                source_validation.py # Reject unsupported syntax before lowering
                call_bindings.py # Static resolution of device-function calls
                ast_transform.py # Python AST → Tack IR
                lowering/        # KernelTransformer's parts: loops, arrays, vectors, inlining, ...
                template_rewrite.py  # AST pre-pass for template parameters
                ir.py            # IR node definitions (30+ node types)
                ir_traversal.py  # walk_ir, transform_ir, clone_ir
                ir_names.py      # Binding names, fresh_name
                ir_verify.py     # verify_ir: invariants at each pass boundary
                ir_bounds.py     # Debug mode's bounds checks: sites, access guards
                ir_resolve.py    # Replace IRDimSize with constants
                ir_optimize.py   # conservative copy propagation
                ir_type_annotate.py  # Annotate expressions with dtype
                ir_pack_scalars.py   # Group scalar params into array buffers
                type_inference.py    # Annotate IR params from actual args
                atomic_support.py    # Atomic target and dtype checks
                workgroup_support.py, workgroup_participation.py  # Workgroup checks
                inspect_kernel.py    # tack.inspect()
                types.py         # ScalarType: f32, i32, i64, etc.
                array.py         # Array, Texture3D
                dlpack.py        # DLPack import/export
            codegen/             # IR → target code
                identifiers.py   # Collision-free target identifiers
                llvm_gen.py      # → LLVM IR (for CPU backend)
                msl_gen.py       # → Metal Shading Language
                cuda_gen.py      # → CUDA C
                hip_gen.py       # → HIP C (extends cuda_gen)
                opencl_gen.py    # → OpenCL C (extends cuda_gen)
                bounds.py        # Debug mode's bounds-check helper (C family)
            runtime/             # Dispatch and device management
                backend.py       # Backend base class: declared capabilities
                kernel_utils.py  # resolve_variant(), the fast path, variant keys, kernel caches
                disk_cache.py    # Lowered IR and compiled variants on disk (tack.cache)
                debug_bounds.py  # Debug mode's hidden arguments and IndexError
                dispatch.py      # devices, the default device, launch placement, tack.sync()
                cpu.py           # CPU backend (llvmlite JIT, threading policy)
                cpu_pool.py      # CPU thread pool, JIT-compiled from LLVM IR
                metal.py         # Metal backend (pyobjc)
                cuda_backend.py  # CUDA backend (cuda-python)
                hip_backend.py   # HIP backend (hip-python)
                level_zero_backend.py # Level Zero backend (ctypes)
            cache.py             # tack.cache: settings, MPI bundles, python -m tack.cache
            algorithms/          # General-purpose parallel primitives
                scan.py          # Parallel prefix sum (exclusive/inclusive)
                copy.py          # copy, fill_value
                stats.py         # Statistics and histograms

    tack-vis/                     # Scientific visualization algorithms
        src/tack/
            dataset/             # Datasets, spaces, views and their algorithms
                algorithms/      # contour, clip, threshold, gradients, ... (one per file)
            interop/             # External framework interop
                vtk.py           # VTK ↔ Tack zero-copy exchange

Both packages share the tack namespace via pkgutil.extend_path; tack-vis depends on tack-core. The path tracer that was tack-rendering is archived under archive/tack-rendering until the dataset API settles.

docs.title: Code Size
docs.text:
tack-core is about 25,100 lines of Python, including docstrings and comments (wc -l over packages/tack-core/src, October 2026); tack-vis adds about 12,400:

Directory Lines Role lang/ ~8,800 Frontend: validation, AST transform, IR, passes, verification codegen/ ~4,500 5 code generators and shared helpers runtime/ ~10,200 5 backend runtimes, variant resolution, disk cache, CPU threading and pool

No C/C++ code. No build step. Everything is pure Python with JIT compilation at runtime.

docs.title: Key Design Decisions
docs.text:
The decisions below are the structural ones. The principles behind them, and the correctness rules the compiler follows, are in Design Principles.

Pure Python throughout. Unlike Taichi (which has a C++ core with pybind11 bindings), Tack implements the entire pipeline in Python. This makes the codebase easy to read, modify, and debug. Kernels run as native code generated by LLVM or the vendor compiler, not through Python; the Python cost is in compilation, paid once per compiled variant, and in per-call dispatch overhead.

Separate IR from codegen. The IR is a simple tree of Python objects (not strings, not LLVM objects). Each codegen backend walks the same IR and emits its own output format. This makes adding a new backend straightforward.

AST-level function inlining. @tack.func calls are inlined by copy-and-rename at the AST level: during IR transformation, each call site lowers a renamed copy of the callee's validated AST. This avoids needing function call support in the IR or any backend.

Template expansion at AST level. @tack.device_class objects are resolved by rewriting the kernel AST before IR transformation. Class-level scalar attributes become constants, instance scalar attributes and array attributes become parameters, and method calls become inlined function bodies. The IR and codegens never see templates.

Non-owning pointer interop. tack.array_from_ptr() wraps external device memory without allocation or copy. Each backend implements wrap_ptr() so that the wrapped memory is never freed by Tack (the CUDA, HIP and Level Zero buffers carry an _owned = False flag). Such arrays are read-only by default, with an explicit writable opt-in. The flag is checked by host-side Array methods and, for kernels, at dispatch: a read-only array bound to a parameter the kernel may store to is refused before the launch. This enables interop with in-situ frameworks (Catalyst), GPU libraries (pycuda, cupy), and cross-library buffer sharing. See Interoperability.

docs.title: AST Transform
docs.text:
The AST transformer (ast_transform.py) converts a Python function's AST into Tack IR. It is the heart of the frontend.

KernelTransformer is one class assembled from mixins, one module each in lang/lowering/, grouped by job. Each sets up the state it owns in its own _init_... method and reaches the others through self:

Module Mixin What it lowers ast_transform.py KernelTransformer the visit_* walk (assignment, calls, subscripts, names, operators) and the expression machinery the others use (_visit_expression, _visit_ordered, _capture_value, _source_error) lowering/loops.py Loops the parallel loop, ndindex, sequential loops, while lowering/arrays.py ArrayAccess indexing and linearization, vector and structure-of-arrays elements lowering/vectors.py VectorValues vector and matrix values, components, methods, scalarized assignment lowering/inlining.py Inlining @tack.func calls, return restructuring, renaming lowering/local_arrays.py LocalArrays tack.shared, tack.local_array lowering/checks.py LoweringChecks checks on emitted IR: effects outside the parallel loop, values left in scalar positions, unbound names lowering/bounds.py BoundsChecks debug mode's IRBoundsCheck (_checked) lowering/values.py — VectorValue and TupleValue

docs.title: Entry Point
docs.text:
# In kernel.py, when get_ir() is called:
from tack.lang.ast_transform import transform_kernel
ir_module = transform_kernel(ast_tree, vector_arrays=..., texture_arrays=...,
                             python_func=kernel.func, template_funcs=...)

transform_kernel creates a KernelTransformer (an ast.NodeVisitor) and visits the module. The result is an IRModule containing one IRFunction.

call_bindings.py supplies static device-call resolution from the defining Python callable and transformation-local template method map. AST-only callers can supply an explicit bindings dictionary. Bare kernel intrinsics remain available without a Python import; device functions require a bound Func object. No global function-name registry is consulted.

Original kernel source is validated by source_validation.py before transformation. Original @tack.func bodies are also validated before return restructuring or variable renaming, so unreachable unsupported syntax cannot disappear. Unsupported constructs raise UnsupportedSyntaxError, a NotImplementedError subclass, with the function name, construct, and line/column in captured, dedented source. The transformer's default visitor also rejects unknown nodes. Docstrings and pass are explicit no-ops; decorators and annotations are host metadata.

docs.title: KernelTransformer State
docs.text:
The transformer tracks several pieces of state:

  • _loop_depth — 0 at the top level. The for i in range(...) at depth 0 becomes IRParallelFor; nested loops become IRSequentialFor.
  • _in_parallel_loop, _parallel_loop_seen and _kernel_body — enforce the one-loop rule and the outside-the-loop rule. _visit_parallel_for accepts one for statement directly in the kernel body; a second one, or one inside a top-level if or while, raises UnsupportedSyntaxError, as does a kernel with none. While _in_parallel_loop is false, _visit_body passes each lowered statement to _check_outside_parallel_loop, which rejects an array store, atomic, barrier, block reduction or print (_effect_name) at the statement's source position. It runs on the lowered IR so effects from inlined device functions and template methods are seen; nested bodies are visited first, so the reported position is the innermost one.
  • _inline_counter — monotonic counter for generating unique variable names during @tack.func inlining.
  • _vector_vars — tracks which local variables are vectors or matrices (name → component count). _matrix_vars holds (rows, columns) for the ones that are matrices. _bind_vector sets both and _variable_value reads them, so use those rather than the dicts.
  • _vector_arrays — tracks which parameters are vector arrays (for scalarization), with _matrix_arrays beside it. The runtime passes a matrix array's entry as a (rows, columns) tuple; the constructor splits it. _array_shape(name) gives an element's shape either way.
  • _texture_arrays — tracks which parameters are textures (for tex.sample()).
  • _texture_origin — maps renamed texture names back to original parameter names (needed when textures pass through @tack.func inlining).
  • _shared_vars — names of tack.shared() and tack.local_array() variables (affects indexing — these are arrays, not scalars).
  • _pre_stmts — statements generated by expression-level inlining that must execute at the expression's original position. Reentrant body traversal preserves the surrounding expression's pending statements.

docs.title: Expression Evaluation
docs.text:
_visit_expression isolates an expression's value and prerequisite statements. _visit_ordered visits operands left to right and materializes earlier loads before a later operand's inlined effects. Boolean and conditional expressions put those prerequisite statements inside IRIf guards, rather than moving them before the guard. Inlined while conditions are lowered into an always-entered loop with condition statements and a guarded break, so continue reevaluates the condition.

Augmented stores reuse a single evaluated address and retain the old load before right-hand-side effects. Sequential range bounds and steps are captured before the loop. CPU codegen also short-circuits pure IRBoolOp and IRIfExp expressions with branches and phi joins. Comparisons and logical expressions yield normalized i32 values 0/1.

See the kernel language contract for the supported subset and numerical decisions still open.

docs.title: Parallel For
docs.text:
At loop depth 0, for i in range(n) becomes:

IRParallelFor(var="i", start=IRConstant(0), end=IRName("n"), body=[...])

With range(start, end, step), Tack transforms the step into a contiguous-index parallel loop with a decomposition assignment:

# for i in range(0, 100, 3) becomes:
# for __step_idx__ in range(0, ceil(100/3)):
#     i = 0 + __step_idx__ * 3

docs.title: Sequential For
docs.text: At loop depth > 0, for loops become IRSequentialFor. The step attribute is preserved (used by codegens for the C for-loop increment). Bounds and steps are captured once before entry. Loops inside while are also sequential. Literal zero and negative steps are rejected; dynamic steps must be positive. A break from the outer parallel loop is rejected, while nested sequential break and both forms of continue are supported.

docs.title: ndindex
docs.text:
A top-level for i, j in tack.ndindex(w, h) (or three dimensions) becomes one IRParallelFor that keeps its dimensions: dims names one index variable per dimension, slowest first, and extents holds their sizes as host-evaluated expressions, like the loop's end (their product). The body starts with i = __nd_0__ and j = __nd_1__ (plus a range's start, for a (start, end) pair), and nothing divides: each backend binds the dimension variables from a launch of the same shape (see lang/parallel_dims.py).

A kernel that uses workgroup primitives, a loop of four or more dimensions, and an ndindex nested inside the parallel loop keep the flat form, a loop over the product whose body recovers the indices:

j = __idx__ % h
i = __idx__ // h

docs.title: Function Call Dispatch
docs.text:
visit_Call is the most complex method. It handles:

  1. Math builtins (sqrt, sin, etc.) → IRCall
  2. tack.atomic_add/min/max → IRAtomicOp
  3. tack.shared(dtype, size) → IRSharedAlloc
  4. tack.local_array(dtype, size) → IRLocalAlloc
  5. tack.barrier() → IRBarrier
  6. tack.thread_id() → IRThreadId
  7. print(...) → IRPrint
  8. int(), float() → IRCast
  9. tex.sample(u, v, w) → IRTextureSample
  10. Vector and matrix methods (.normalized(), .dot(), .cross(), .sum(), .transpose(), .inverse(), ...) → scalarized ops, in _emit_vector_method and _emit_matrix_method
  11. tack.vec2/vec3/vec4(...) → a VectorValue (_visit_vector_construct); tack.mat2/mat3/mat4(...), tack.mat(row, ...), tack.identity(n) → a VectorValue with a two-dimensional shape (_visit_matrix_construct, _visit_matrix_identity)
  12. @tack.func calls → inlined via _inline_func_call
